sentence: A high white blood cell count is a non-specific sign, most often from infection, and doctors read it with the type of cell raised.
note: LTO/MedlinePlus: raised WBC non-specific; infection most common cause

sentence: NHS inform says a full blood count checks the types and numbers of cells in the blood, including red cells, white cells and platelets.
The test gives a total white cell count and a differential that splits white cells into types.
Those types include neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils.
Neutrophils are the main defence against bacterial infection.
A raised count is a non-specific signal, which means it does not point to one cause.
A high count can indicate infection, inflammation, or leukaemia and other blood disorders.
Infection, most often bacterial infection, is the most common cause.
Results vary with age and time of day, and older people sometimes do not show a raised count even when they have an infection.
Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis can raise the count, and so can allergies.
Some medicines, for example corticosteroids, can raise it.
Tissue damage such as burns can raise it.
Severe physical or emotional stress, for example from an injury or surgery, can raise it.
Smoking and pregnancy can also raise the count.
A high neutrophil count usually suggests bacterial infection, inflammation or physical stress on the body.
A high lymphocyte count can occur with viral infections or with conditions such as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
Leukaemia and Hodgkin disease can cause persistently high counts, which is why doctors follow up unexplained rises.
A hospital guideline from Hampshire says a mild, lasting rise is likely to come from a chronic inflammatory or infective process, or from smoking.
The same guideline says an unexplained, very high count prompts an urgent referral to haematology.
Doctors read the count with symptoms, the differential and sometimes a repeat test or a blood film.
Reference ranges differ with age, sex and laboratory, so the report shows the range used.
Feeling unwell with a fever is a reason to contact NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and severe breathing difficulty or collapse needs a 999 call.
A GP may order a blood test if leukaemia is suspected, and a very high number of abnormal white cells can point towards it.
In that case the person is referred urgently to a specialist in blood conditions, called a haematologist.
Symptoms listed by the NHS across leukaemia types include tiredness, bleeding or bruising easily, night sweats, weight loss and frequent infections.
The NHS stresses that having these symptoms does not mean someone has leukaemia, and that many are caused by more common conditions.
For chronic myeloid leukaemia the NHS advises a non-urgent GP visit if symptoms appear.
A high white cell count can be caused by infection, inflammation, some medicines, stress or smoking, and less often by a blood disorder.
The differential count shows which type of white cell is raised, which helps narrow down the cause.
A mild, lasting rise is often linked to chronic inflammation, infection or smoking, while an unexplained very high count leads to urgent referral to haematology.
A single high count does not diagnose anything, and doctors may repeat the test.
